content: Microwaves are a type of electromagnetic wave characterized by wavelengths shorter than one meter but longer than one millimeter, corresponding to frequencies between 300 megahertz (MHz) and 300 gigahertz (GHz). These frequencies are categorized into ultra-high frequency (UHF), super high frequency (SHF), and extremely high frequency (EHF) bands. The term microwave is used when the wavelength of the signal is comparable to the physical dimensions of the equipment used, making traditional lumped-element circuit theory inadequate. Instead, microwave engineering relies on distributed circuit elements and transmission-line theory. Waveguides often replace coaxial or open-wire transmission lines, and cavity resonators or resonant lines are used instead of lumped-element tuned circuits. Phenomena such as reflection, polarization, scattering, diffraction, and atmospheric absorption, typically associated with visible light, are also significant in microwave propagation. While the term microwave might suggest micrometer-scale wavelengths, it more accurately refers to wavelengths much smaller than those used in traditional radio broadcasting. The boundaries between microwaves, millimeter waves, terahertz radiation, and far-infrared light are not rigid and vary across different scientific disciplines. The existence of electromagnetic waves, including microwaves, was first predicted by James Clerk Maxwell in 1864 through his equations. Heinrich Hertz experimentally confirmed their existence in 1888 by generating and detecting microwaves in the UHF range using rudimentary materials like a horse trough and a parabolic zinc gutter as an antenna. In 1894, Jagadish Chandra Bose demonstrated the use of millimeter waves for radio control of a bell and conducted further research into microwave propagation. Microwave sources include vacuum tube devices such as magnetrons, klystrons, traveling wave tubes (TWTs), and gyrotrons. These devices operate based on the ballistic motion of electron clumps under the influence of electric or magnetic fields, rather than a continuous electron stream. Masers, which are similar to lasers but operate at microwave frequencies, are another source of microwaves. Microwaves have a wide range of applications: 1. Communication: Before fiber optics, long-distance telephone calls were transmitted via microwave point-to-point links. Starting in the 1950s, frequency division multiplexing allowed thousands of telephone channels to be transmitted on a single microwave channel. Wireless LAN protocols, such as Bluetooth and IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi), use the 2.4 GHz ISM band, while 802.11a operates in the 5 GHz range. Metropolitan Area Networks (MANs), like WiMAX, operate in the 2–11 GHz range, with commercial implementations in the 2.5 GHz, 3.5 GHz, and 5.8 GHz bands. Wide Area Mobile Broadband Wireless Access (MBWA) protocols, such as IEEE 802.20, operate between 1.6 and 2.3 GHz, offering mobility and in-building penetration similar to mobile phones but with higher spectral efficiency. Cable TV, Internet access, and some mobile phone networks (e.g., GSM) use lower microwave frequencies. Microwaves are also used in television broadcasting to transmit signals from remote locations to stations using highly directive antennas, which are smaller and more practical due to the short wavelength of microwaves. 2. Remote Sensing: Radar systems use microwaves to detect the range, speed, and characteristics of distant objects. Radar technology, which saw significant development during World War II, is now used in air traffic control, ship navigation, and speed enforcement. Radio astronomy relies heavily on microwaves to study celestial phenomena. Microwave imaging is used in biomedical applications, such as photoacoustic imaging. 3. Navigation: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), including GPS and GLONASS, transmit navigational signals in the 1.2–1.6 GHz range. 4. Power Applications: Microwave ovens operate at approximately 2.45 GHz, using dielectric heating to heat food by exciting water, fat, and sugar molecules. These appliances became widespread in the late 1970s. Industrial processes use microwave heating for drying and curing materials. Semiconductor manufacturing employs microwaves to generate plasma for processes like reactive ion etching and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). Microwaves can transmit power over long distances. NASA explored the concept of solar power satellites in the 1970s and 1980s, which would beam energy to Earth via microwaves. Non-lethal weapons, such as the Active Denial System, use millimeter waves to heat the outer layer of human skin, causing discomfort and forcing individuals to move away. A focused 95 GHz beam can heat the skin to 130°F (54°C) at a depth of 0.4 mm. The microwave spectrum is generally defined as electromagnetic energy with frequencies between 1 GHz and 1000 GHz, though most practical applications fall within the 1–40 GHz range. Frequency bands within this range are designated by specific letter names, such as L, S, C, X, Ku, K, and Ka bands. Microwaves are a form of non-ionizing radiation, meaning they lack sufficient energy to ionize atoms or molecules. While the term radiation often causes concern, it simply refers to the emission of energy. Numerous studies over the past two decades have concluded that microwaves are safe for use under regulated conditions. The term microwave was first formally documented in 1931. In 1946, the term was used in an astronomical context in a paper titled Microwave Radiation from the Sun and Moon by Robert Dicke and Robert Beringer. The development of microwave technology owes much to the foundational work of figures like James Clerk Maxwell, Heinrich Hertz, Jagadish Chandra Bose, and others who contributed to the understanding and application of electromagnetic theory.
